newsitem.title: UK: Tsarist bond holders fail to hold Russia to ransom.
newsitem.headline: Tsarist bond holders fail to hold Russia to ransom.

text.p: French investors' attempts to hold Russia to ransom for pre-revolutionary debt have made little impact on the success of Russia's debut Eurobond, launched last week, analysts said.

The French were among the biggest investors in Tsarist Russia, and Russian Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin was meeting French President Jacques Chirac on Tuesday in a bid to resolve a dispute over the debt.
Successors of the original French buyers claim around 140-160 billion French francs ($27.35-31.26 billion) on the Tsarist debt, mainly in unpaid interest.
But a Moscow-based analyst told Reuters Financial Television on Tuesday Russia was unlikely to pay French holders of the Tsarist-era bonds more than $125 million.

"French holders will be lucky if they get more than about three cents on the dollar for the bonds, which makes a total of around $125 million," Roland Nash, chief economist at Renaissance Capital, said in a telephone interview.
The nominal value of the Tsarist bonds was about $30 billion but the amount actually still in existence was only about 13 percent of that total, he said.

The spread on the $1.0 billion five-year Russian Eurobond has remained steady at Thursday's launch level of 345 basis points over U.S. Treasury notes. The deal was twice oversubscribed following extensive global presentations.

"Just because a few French families happen to hold a few (Tsarist) bonds they are trying to hold everybody, including a country, to ransom," a senior Eastern European specialist at a major German bank in Frankfurt said.
"At the end of the day the Russians might make some type of gesture, but I would not advise them to do any more than that."
Other Russian debt such as MinFin bonds and Vneshekonombank debt were also unaffected by the French investors' demands.

Analysts in London said Russia might feel forced to clear the air so as to join the Paris club of official creditors to negotiate the return of some of the money it lent in the days of the Soviet Union.

But they said that from a legal point of view it was a moot point whether the Soviet Union was the rightful heir to the Bolshevik debt, which predates the 1917 Revolution, and in turn whether the Russian Federation should inherit the Soviet debt.

"Eurobond investors don't really care what's happening with the Tsarist bonds, it's a mute issue, it won't have an affect either way, its a French domestic issue anyway," a debt origination manager at a U.S. bank said.
In October Russian finance minister Alexander Livshits said a reimbursement as a "symbolic gesture" for Tsarist debts which were neglected by the Soviet Union government was close.
A decision by the Paris bourse to temporarily suspend listing of Russian debt on Monday generated ripples of reaction.
But a syndicate manager close to Russia's Eurobond said this had little impact on the paper, which was not listed in Paris because of standard Eurobond selling restrictions.
The only French investors who held the Eurobond paper had it in offshore accounts.

"French investors for a dollar-denominated emerging market transaction are never going to be major, but many of these institutions have offshore branches," the syndicate manager said. "It is a lot of political noise."
Before the launch of the Eurobond last Thursday, French bondholders took out advertisements in major European newspapers urging investors not to buy the issue.

There were no French banks in the syndicate group of six co-lead managers and 10 co-managers. J.P. Morgan and SBC Warburg were the joint lead managers who held the bulk of the paper of around $800 million.
Market makers said the Tsarist bond holders' attempts to get repaid was not helping Russia to solve its economic problems.
